pages.text: In the middle of Wa, the capital of the Upper West Region, stands a white palace that looks like a fortress made of sand. Its walls are thick mud, smoothed and painted, with tall buttresses that end in points. This is the palace of the Wa Naa, the king of the Wala people. Every year, at the Dumba festival, crowds gather in front of it to watch the king perform one act. A cow is tied on the ground, and the Wa Naa must step over it. If he does so cleanly, the people cheer, for the year ahead will be good.

pages.text: Long before there was a king, there were farmers. The first people of the Wa area lived in scattered family settlements. They had no chief over them all. Their leaders were earth priests, who looked after the land and its shrines and decided who could farm where. Their descendants are still called the Tendaamba, the owners of the land. Then, perhaps four hundred years ago, strangers arrived. From the east came mounted princes of the royal families of Mamprugu and Dagbon. From the north-west came Muslim traders and teachers whose ancestors had lived in old Mali.

pages.alt: A farming settlement of flat-roofed mud houses with an elder pouring water at the foot of a large tree.

pages.text: Each group had something that the others lacked. The princes had horses and skill in war and government. The Muslims could read and write, and they traded with distant markets. The Tendaamba knew the land and had the right to bless it. In time, the three made one kingdom. The princes provided the king, the Wa Naa, and the chiefs. The Muslims provided teachers, advisers, and the imam who prayed for the king. The Tendaamba kept charge of the land, and no Wa Naa could be properly installed without their part in the ceremony.

pages.alt: Three men standing together: a horseman in a smock, a scholar holding a writing board, and an elder holding a hoe.

pages.text: Wa became known for learning. Children studied in Qur’anic schools, writing their lessons on wooden boards with ink made from soot. Scholars copied books by hand and wrote down the history of the town in Arabic. Small mud mosques with wooden poles in their walls were built in Wa and in nearby villages such as Nakore, and some still stand. Caravans passing between the forest and the River Niger stopped here. The kingship did not stay in one family. It passed in turn among several royal houses, called gates, so that each had hope of its turn.

pages.text: The 1890s brought danger. Armed bands on horseback were raiding the north for captives. One force was led by Babatu. Another, stronger one belonged to Samori Toure, a ruler from the west who was fighting the French. At the same time, Britain and France were racing to claim land. In 1894, a Fante surveyor named George Ekem Ferguson came to Wa and signed a treaty for the British. He returned in 1897 with a small force. Samori’s army attacked. Ferguson was wounded and killed near Wa. The next year, the British took control.

pages.text: Wa is now a busy regional capital with a university, yet the three old groups are still recognised: the royals, the Muslim community, and the owners of the land. Their story offers a lesson. A country is made of people who arrived at different times and who believe different things. It holds together when each group is given a real part to play and none is told that it does not belong. The Wala worked this out centuries ago. Ghana, with its many peoples, languages, and faiths, depends on the same understanding.

activities.question: Who were the Tendaamba?
options: The first settlers, whose earth priests looked after the land

activities.question: What did the Muslim community contribute to the Wala kingdom?
options: Teachers, advisers, trade links, and the imam

activities.question: How was the kingship of Wa passed on?
options: It rotated among several royal houses called gates
It always went to the eldest son

activities.question: Apply it: A new school has pupils from three different towns. Using the lesson of Wa, what would help them become one school?
options: Let the pupils of one town make all the decisions
Give each group a real part to play in running the school
Keep the groups in separate classrooms

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Farmers led by earth priests settle the Wa area
The three groups form the Wala kingdom
Ferguson signs a treaty at Wa for the British
Samori’s army attacks and Ferguson is killed
